abstract: Endometrium is suspectable to severe injury due to recurrent abortion, curettage or intrauterine infection which could lead to pathological conditions and sabotage women's fertility. Promoting endometrium regeneration is the core of the treatments to uterine related infertility. Patients who received traditional treatments can only expect limited effects, thereby novel therapies are badly in need to promote endometrium regeneration. Here we generated a decellularized extracellular matrix (ECM) from porcine dermis, and composited adipose stem cell derived exosomes (ADSC-exos) on it (ECM@ADSC-exos). In vitro experiments proved that ECM@ADSC-exos exhibited good cytocompatibility and could improve cell proliferation, migration and angiogenesis. We also observed that, when implanted in the uterine cavity of a rat model of endometrium injury, ECM@ADSC-exos improved endometrium regeneration, enhanced local angiogenesis, promoted myometrium repair and finally preserved fertility. Our results proved that ECM@ADSC-exos could be a novel option for endometrium regeneration.

Materials and methods
2.1
Materials
Porcine Endothelial Cell Growth Factor (VEGF) ELISA Kit was purchased from DuMa Biotechnology Co. (Shanghai, China). LIVE/DEAD Backlight bacterial viability kit and Phalloidin were obtained from Invitrogen Co. (USA). Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) kit and bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay kit were obtained from Beyotime Biotechnology Co. (Shanghai, China). The primary antibodies of Ki67, CD31 and α-SMA were obtained from Affinity (China). DyLight®550-labeled Donkey Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies were purchased from Boster Biotechnology Co. (Wuhan, China).
2.2
Porcine skin decellularization and characterization
Extracellular matrix was fabricated using porcine skin. Briefly, the epidermal layer and subcutaneous fat of the porcine skin was removed to obtain dermis. All the porcine dermis was cut into squares of 1 cm × 1 cm. Then the porcine dermis was micronized into a particular size less than 100 μm in a Cryo-mill (Retsch GmbH, Germany). Micronized porcine dermis (MPD) was virus-inactivated and sterilized by 0.3 % peracetic acid for 18 h, and then the MPD was centrifuged and cleaned with a shaking bath in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and circulated 3 times in turn. The MPD decellularized in 1.0 % sodium deoxycholate for 24 h, as well as washed in PBS for 5 times (30 min each) to obtain ECM. The ECM was stored frozen at −20 °C until further use.
The morphologies and macrostructure of the extracellular matrix (ECM) were analyzed by emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, SU-8030, Hitachi, Japan) at 5 kV, following sputter coating with gold. The fixed specimens were subsequently subjected to dehydration using a standard graded series of ethanol, embedded in paraffin blocks, and sectioned into 5-μm-thick slices. These sections were then stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) and examined microscopically (Olympus Inc., Tokyo, Japan).
The extent of decellularization was determined through the quantification of DNA from the ECM. The DNA residue of the ECM was detected by extracting the DNA from 50 mg granules of each sample using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN). The concentration of DNA was measured using Picogreen analysis (Invitrogen) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. The manufacturer-provided control samples were utilized to establish a standard curve. The fluorescence microplate reader (Bio-Rad 680, USA) was employed to quantitatively measure the fluorescence of each sample at excitation/emission (ex/em) wavelengths of
485/
530 nm, and the DNA content was subsequently calculated.
The quantification of collagen content In ECM was performed through the determination of Hydroproline (HYP) levels. The tissue samples were subjected to incubation with 6 M HCl at 105 °C overnight, both before and after decellularization. Following hydrolysis, the resultant samples were neutralized and oxidized with chloramine T. The samples were then reacted with p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde for 20 min in a 60 °C water bath, and the HYP concentration was measured at 558 nm using a microplate reader. The collagen content was evaluated by determining the average amount of collagen containing 13.5 % hydroxyproline.
To detect the lipid content, both untreated and treated tissue underwent hydrolysis using 6 M HCl at 80 °C until complete digestion. The resulting fat was extracted with anhydrous ether and subjected to oven drying until a constant weight was achieved. The weight of the residual fat was subsequently measured using an analytical scale (Mettler Toledo, United States).
The quantification of EGF、FGF and VEGF content within decellularized ECM was conducted through the utilization of a Growth Factor ELISA Kit (DuMa Biotechnology Co., Shanghai, China). The tissue was subjected to the addition of an appropriate volume of saline and subsequently ground for a duration of 10 min. The resultant mixture was subjected to centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. A volume of 10 μL of the supernatant was added to the wells of the ELISA plate, followed by the addition of 100 μL of HRP binding reagent. The ELISA plate was then covered with a gel strip and incubated at a temperature of 37 °C for a duration of 60 min. Following incubation, the ELISA plate underwent five rounds of washing with a washing solution. Subsequently, 100 μL of chromogen solution was introduced to each well and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C in a dark environment. The optical densities (ODs) of each well were measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. A calibration curve was constructed based on the EGF、FGF and VEGF standard provided by the manufacturer, and the concentrations of growth factor for each individual sample were determined by reference to the calibration curve.
The quantification of ECM degradation rate was accomplished through the measurement of HYP levels. ECM samples were placed in separate ET tubes containing 1 mL of Simulated Body Fluid (SBF) or 1 mL SBF (10U/mL type I Collagenase), and subjected to constant temperature agitation (37 °C, 60 rpm). At various time intervals, the solutions were extracted from the ET tubes and replenished with 1 mL of SBF. The concentration of hydroxyproline in each solution was determined using a hydroxyproline detection method.
ECM samples were subjected to mass spectrometry-based proteomics analysis. The STRING v10.0 database (Version:11.5,
https://cn.string-db.org/
) was used to identify protein–protein interactions of ECM, and k-means clustering was used to cluster.
2.3
Isolation, culture and characterization of ADSCs
ADSCs were isolated from subcutaneous inguinal adipose tissue samples obtained from 4-week-old C57BL/6 mice. The tissue was digested in NB4 collagenase solution (Nordmark, Uetersen, Germany) in DMEM supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA) and 1 % streptomycin/penicillin (Sigma, MO, USA). The samples were agitated for 1 h at 250 rpm and 37 °C, and the resulting cells were collected, transferred to tissue culture dishes, and cultured until they had undergone three passages before being utilized for downstream experiments.
2.4
Production and isolation of exosomes
The isolation of exosomes was carried out in accordance with established protocols. Specifically, at a point when ADSCs had achieved 50–60 % confluence, the culture medium was replaced. Upon reaching 90–100 % confluence, 40 mL of supernatant was collected from the ADSCs and subjected to centrifugation at 500
g
for 10 min at 4 °C to eliminate suspended cells. The resulting supernatant was then subjected to further centrifugation at 1.2 × 10
4
g for 20 min at 4 °C to eliminate cellular debris and apoptotic bodies. The supernatant was collected and subsequently subjected to centrifugation at 1 × 10
5
g for 70 min at 4 °C. The resulting sediment was re-suspended in PBS and subjected to ultracentrifugation (1 × 10
5
g) for 70 min at 4 °C to eliminate any contaminating proteins. The suspension of exosomes derived from ADSCs (100 μL from 2 × 10
7
cells) was obtained by re-suspending the collected sediment in PBS and stored at −80 °C for future use.
2.5
Characterization of exosomes
The morphology of exosomes was examined using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai 12, Philips, Netherlands). Initially, 20 μL of exosomes was placed on a carbon film and incubated for 5 min. Subsequently, the sample was negatively stained with 2 % uranyl acetate and air-dried for imaging. The protein content of exosomes was quantified using a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo), while the size distribution and concentration of exosomes were determined by nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA, Nanosight NS300, Malvern Instruments). The samples were slowly introduced into the sample chamber. Three movie recordings were captured then the mean value was determined.
Western blot analysis was performed using exosomal markers CD63 (1:500; ab134045, Abcam) and CD9 (1:500; ab236630, Abcam). The proteins were separated by gel electrophoresis using NuPAGE 4–12 % Bis-Tris (Invitrogen) and subsequently transferred onto a polyvinylidene fluoride membrane (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) for immunoblotting with specific primary antibodies. The bands were detected using a secondary anti-rabbit antibody (1:3000; Dawen, Hangzhou, China) and Immobilon Western Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (Millipore, Boston, MA, USA).
2.6
Flow cytometry
The ADSC-derived exosomes were suspended in isolation buffer and subsequently mixed with magnetic CD9 Dynabeads® for a duration of 10 min. This was followed by an overnight incubation at 4 °C and a 1-h incubation at room temperature. The unbound exosomes were separated using a magnet. The remaining bead-bound exosomes were washed twice in a 200 μL volume of isolation buffer and resuspended in isolation buffer (200 μL). Subsequently, they were incubated with anti-CD63 (1:500; ab134045, Abcam) and anti-CD9 (1:500; ab236630, Abcam) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by centrifugation for 1 min at 8000 g. After discarding the supernatants, the labeled exosomes were resuspended in PBS and subsequently labeled with an appropriate AF488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; Abcam). The resulting samples were subjected to an additional minute of centrifugation at 8000
g
, and the supernatants were discarded. Following two washes with PBS, the pellets were resuspended in 100 μL PBS. The exosome staining was assessed using a FACS Canto II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).
2.7
Cell culture
The Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) were cultured inDMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS and 1 % penicillin and streptomycin. The cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
, with medium changes performed every two days.
2.8
Cell viability assay
In accordance with the manufacturer's agreement, the viability of HUVECs was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 to evaluate the cytotoxicity of various samples (ECM, ADSC-Exos, ECM@ADSC-Exos). Firstly, extracts of different materials were conducted in a ratio of 0.1g to 1 mL in the same culture medium for 24 h, then the supernatants were collected and filtered using 0.22 μm filter membranes. The cells were seeded at a density of 1 × 10
4
cells/well and cultured in DMEM extraction solutions of different materials at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for 24 h. Upon reaching the designated time point, the cells were washed thrice with PBS to eliminate DMEM containing 10 % FBS, and subsequently supplemented with fresh medium (200 μL per well, containing 20 μL CCK-8 solution per well). The cells were subsequently incubated at a temperature of 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for a duration of 2 h, following which the OD values were measured at a wavelength of 450 nm using a microplate reader.
After a period of 24 h, the media was removed and the cells were rinsed thrice with PBS. Subsequently, the cells were incubated with 100 μL Calcein/PI dilutions at room temperature for 30 min in the absence of light. Finally, the images were captured using a Leica upright fluorescence microscope (DM6B).
2.9
HUVEC proliferation, migration, and tube formation assays
To evaluate proliferation, HUVECs (4 × 10
4
) were introduced to the lower chamber, while the upper chamber received 200 mg of ECM, 20 μg of ADSC-Exos, or a combination of both. Ki67 immunofluorescent staining was employed to assess HUVEC proliferation. Specifically, cells were washed thrice with PBS for 5 min each time, fixed with 4 % Paraformaldehyde for 15 min, and then washed thrice with PBS for 5 min each time. To enhance the permeability of the membrane, a 0.5 % (v/v) Triton X-100 in PBS solution was used to permeabilize the cells for a duration of 20 min. Subsequently, the cells were blocked with 1 % (v/v) goat serum for 60 min at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation at 4 °C with an antibody targeting Ki67. The following day, the cells were subjected to a 2-h incubation with phalloidin staining solution and secondary antibody. Finally, the cells were washed and stained with DAPI for 5 min, and the samples were visualized using fluorescence microscopy.
For the migration assays, 4 × 10
4
HUVECs were introduced to the upper chamber of a Transwell assay filter. The lower chamber was supplemented with 200 mg of ECM, 20 μg of ADSC-Exos, or a combination of both. The cells were cultured for 18 h at 37 °C, followed by fixation and staining of the cells on the upper chamber membrane using 0.5 % crystal violet for subsequent microscopic quantification.
To assess the impact of ADSC-Exos on HUVEC tube formation, HUVECs were cultured in DMEM extraction solutions of varying compositions for a duration of 6 h. Subsequently, the morphological alterations of HUVECs were examined under a microscope. Matrigel (50 μL) was placed in a 96-well plate and allowed to solidify at 37 °C for 30 min. HUVECs (0.8 × 10
4
cells/100 μL) were suspended in serum-free medium and added to the Matrigel-coated wells. The cell suspensions were then incubated at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for 24 h. The specimen was subjected to observation and photographic documentation under an optical microscope at hourly intervals until the conclusion of the experiment. The quantification and measurement of tube lengths were conducted using ImageJ software and subjected to statistical analysis via the ANOVA-test.
The Transwell assay filters were utilized in a co-culture system to evaluate the proliferation, migration, and tube formation capacity of HUVECs.
2.10
Animal model
The Experimental Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine granted approval for the animal experiments, with license number (2020) No. (139). A total of 30 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (SD rats; average weight 250 g), procured from the Experimental Animal Institute of Medical College of Zhejiang University, were randomly assigned to five groups: Blank (n = 6), Control (n = 6), ADSC-Exos (n = 6), ECM (n = 6), and ECM@ ADSC-Exos (n = 6). A model of rodent thin endometrium was established by means of injecting anhydrous ethanol into the uterus, as previously described. In brief, all rats were subjected to anesthesia via intraperitoneal injection of 2 % sodium pentobarbital (0.3 mL/100 g), and the uterine horns were exposed through an abdominal incision. The proximal and distal portions of the uterus were subsequently clamped with two vascular clamps, following which 95 % ethanol was injected into the uterine cavity for a duration of 60 s. Blank group animals were injected with 100 μL PBS in the uterine horn. The vascular clamps were subsequently released and delicately compressed to eliminate any residual ethanol, and the affected areas were rinsed with PBS thrice to further eliminate any remaining ethanol. The experimental group of animals underwent reoperation after model development, wherein one end of the uterus was clipped, and the experimental group materials were injected into the uterine cavity via syringe from the other end. ADSC-Exos group was injected with 100 μL PBS containing 10 μg of ADSC-Exos; ECM group injection 100 μL PBS containing 100 mg of ECM; ECM@ ADSC-Exos group injection 100 μL PBS containing 100 mg of ECM@ADSC-Exos. Following the injection of materials, the rats underwent three estrus cycles before being euthanized, and their uterine tissues were excised and sectioned or frozen as appropriate for downstream analyses.
2.11
Histological evaluation
The assessment of endometrial fibrosis involved initial fixation of excised tissue sections in 4 % paraformaldehyde for an overnight period, followed by demineralization utilizing 16 % ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, and subsequent embedding in OCT. The sections were then subjected to routine H&E and Masson's trichrome staining.
2.12
Immunohistochemical staining
The present study utilized immunohistochemical staining to evaluate the levels of endometrial fibrosis and angiogenesis. Specifically, 20 μm-thick sections were initially blocked with 5 % BSA, and subsequently incubated overnight with rabbit anti-CD31 (1:100; ab28364, Abcam) and rabbit anti-α-SMA (1:100; ab108531, Abcam) at 4 °C. Following three washes with PBS, the sections were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with secondary goat anti-rabbit IgG, and finally observed under an optical microscope.
2.13
Fertility testing
The evaluation of endometrial receptivity was predicated on the capacity of the endometrium to facilitate the implantation of a fertilized embryo and to provide adequate nourishment for fetal development. The rat estrus cycle status was determined through a vaginal smear method. Twenty female rats were selected from each of the five treatment groups outlined above and were subjected to mating with sexually mature male rats at a 1:1 ratio on the day of estrus. The presence or absence of a vaginal plug was subsequently evaluated the following morning. At 18 days post vaginal plug appearance, fetal numbers, size, and weight were assessed in each group, as were embryo locations.
2.14
Statistical analysis
Data in the present study were expressed as mean ± S.D. (standard deviation), and
p
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical evaluation was performed by one-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey test for multiple comparisons.

Materials
Porcine Endothelial Cell Growth Factor (VEGF) ELISA Kit was purchased from DuMa Biotechnology Co. (Shanghai, China). LIVE/DEAD Backlight bacterial viability kit and Phalloidin were obtained from Invitrogen Co. (USA). Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) kit and bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay kit were obtained from Beyotime Biotechnology Co. (Shanghai, China). The primary antibodies of Ki67, CD31 and α-SMA were obtained from Affinity (China). DyLight®550-labeled Donkey Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies were purchased from Boster Biotechnology Co. (Wuhan, China).

1
Introduction
The endometrium plays a crucial role in embryo implantation and development [
1
]. However, detrimental factors such as hysteromyomectomy, curettage and endometritis can lead to endometrial injury [
2
], resulting in abnormal uterine bleeding, miscarriage, pregnancy complications or infertility [
3
]. The current clinical treatment methods, including delivery of cytokines and exogenous estrogen, can repair the thickness of the damaged endometrial wall to a certain extent [
4
], but cannot restore its original structure and function [
5
,
6
]. Se–Ra et al. found that although luteinizing hormone promoted endometrial regeneration, the receptivity and fertility of the regenerated endometrial wall were significantly reduced, leading to premature birth or miscarriage [
7
]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new treatments that can not only repair the damaged endometrial structure but also enhance the receptivity of the endometrium, thereby increasing the chances of embryo implantation and the birth of a healthy newborn.
Stem cells, as a special type of cells with self-renewal ability and multi-directional differentiation potential, are widely used in the clinical treatment of various diseases [
8
]. Bone marrow-derived stem cells (BMSCs) [
9
], adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs)[
25
], and umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) can promote the regeneration and repair of damaged endometrium by differentiating into endometrial epithelial cells and stromal cells [
10
,
11
]. However, the challenges and risks of stem cell therapy should not be ignored, including the need for a continuous source of phenotypically stable cells, the risk of immune-mediated rejection, and the limitations of stem cell loss and uncontrolled differentiation [
12
]. Recent studies have shown that the key factor for stem cell-driven tissue repair may be the paracrine signals they mediate, rather than their differentiation ability [
13
]. Exosomes play a crucial role in this process. Stem cell-derived exosomes can deliver proteins, mRNAs, miRNAs, and other molecules to proximal or distal cells, effectively propagating the regenerative signals from stem cells [
14
]. Compared with stem cells, exosomes have superior biosafety, less immune response, low risk of rejection, and ease to store, transport, and use [
15
]. At present, exosomes derived from adipose mesenchymal stem cells (ADSC-Exos) have been shown to play a significant role in the field of endometrial regeneration[
16
]. Specifically, the administration of ADSC exosomes significantly promotes angiogenesis and increases glandular density, thereby facilitating endometrial regeneration and inhibiting local tissue fibrosis, ultimately leading to the restoration of partial fertility[
14
]. However, the short half-life of exosomes
in vivo
is relatively short as they tend to be cleared by host cells once administrated [
14
]. Therefore, developing a delivery system that can effectively bind exosomes and achieve long-term release has become a key issue in achieving damaged endometrial regeneration.
Naturally derived biomacromolecules such as chitosan, collagen and others have long been exploited for biomedical purposes. Extracellular matrix (ECM) is the three-dimensional network composed of extracellular macromolecules, which play an important role in cell migration, differentiation, and proliferation [
17
]. Various tissues such as skin, small intestinal submucosa, and bone have been use for decellularization to obtain ECM-based biological scaffolds with active biochemical signals for directing cell growth, migration, and differentiation [
18
]. ECM is usually in a natural cross-linked state and can actively degrade under the action of proteinases secreted by cells, achieving precise matching of tissue regeneration and scaffold degradation rates to promote tissue repair [
19
]. Besides acting as a scaffold material to guide tissue regeneration, ECM also serves as an effective reservoir for growth factor binding and store while also provides a protective function during tissue metabolism. Specifically, ECM possesses extraordinary affinity to biological components such as growth factor, cytokines, and exosomes as extracellular proteins such as collagen, as well as proteoglycan provide abundant binding motifs for these molecules and vesicles [
19
]. Recent studies have shown that by combining biomaterials with exosomes, the loading rate of exosomes can be effectively improved and long-term release can be achieved [
14
,
15
]. Although ECM delivery systems have been employed for growth factor, stem cell and gene therapy to facilitate the regeneration of endometrium [
20
][
[12]
,
[15]
,
[25]
], delivery of exosome via ECM material has not been reported in the research on endometrial regeneration.
In this study, we utilized the superior biologics loading capacity of ECM and the functionality of embedded exosomes to construct an ECM/ADSC-Exos delivery system. We aimed to achieve sustained release of ADSC-Exos by loading ADSC-Exos onto micronized ECM, meanwhile providing regenerative cues by forming a scaffolding ECM layer on the surface of injured endometrium during the endometrial healing process. Firstly, decellularized porcine dermis was micronized to generate the micronized ECM, then ADSC-Exos were bound onto the micronized ECM through electrostatic interaction between ECM binding motifs and Exo surface, forming an ECM delivery system endowed with sustained exosome release feature, as well as cell-infiltration scaffold targeting at the injured surface of endometrium. This delivery system not only overcame the short half-life of ADSC-Exos
in vivo
through immobilization onto ECM and allow sustained release of ADSC-Exos, but also provide intrinsic instructive cues for tissue regeneration via inductive signals preserved in ECM. Besides, our previous study also demonstrated that angiogenic factors such as VEGF significantly promoted local angiogenesis once ECM was implant[
18
], thus such delivery system is also expected to enhance the vascularization of injured endometrium. Moreover, this system exhibited excellent injectability, degradability, and biosafety, making it easy for minimally invasive injection into the uterine cavity. In summary, this study provides a new alternative for vascularized endometrial regeneration through optimized exosome delivery and intrinsic inductive cues from ECM (see
Fig. 1
).

The ADSC-derived exosomes were suspended in isolation buffer and subsequently mixed with magnetic CD9 Dynabeads® for a duration of 10 min. This was followed by an overnight incubation at 4 °C and a 1-h incubation at room temperature. The unbound exosomes were separated using a magnet. The remaining bead-bound exosomes were washed twice in a 200 μL volume of isolation buffer and resuspended in isolation buffer (200 μL). Subsequently, they were incubated with anti-CD63 (1:500; ab134045, Abcam) and anti-CD9 (1:500; ab236630, Abcam) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by centrifugation for 1 min at 8000 g. After discarding the supernatants, the labeled exosomes were resuspended in PBS and subsequently labeled with an appropriate AF488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; Abcam). The resulting samples were subjected to an additional minute of centrifugation at 8000
g
, and the supernatants were discarded. Following two washes with PBS, the pellets were resuspended in 100 μL PBS. The exosome staining was assessed using a FACS Canto II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).
2.7
Cell culture
The Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) were cultured inDMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS and 1 % penicillin and streptomycin. The cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
, with medium changes performed every two days.
2.8
Cell viability assay
In accordance with the manufacturer's agreement, the viability of HUVECs was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 to evaluate the cytotoxicity of various samples (ECM, ADSC-Exos, ECM@ADSC-Exos). Firstly, extracts of different materials were conducted in a ratio of 0.1g to 1 mL in the same culture medium for 24 h, then the supernatants were collected and filtered using 0.22 μm filter membranes. The cells were seeded at a density of 1 × 10
4
cells/well and cultured in DMEM extraction solutions of different materials at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for 24 h. Upon reaching the designated time point, the cells were washed thrice with PBS to eliminate DMEM containing 10 % FBS, and subsequently supplemented with fresh medium (200 μL per well, containing 20 μL CCK-8 solution per well). The cells were subsequently incubated at a temperature of 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for a duration of 2 h, following which the OD values were measured at a wavelength of 450 nm using a microplate reader.
After a period of 24 h, the media was removed and the cells were rinsed thrice with PBS. Subsequently, the cells were incubated with 100 μL Calcein/PI dilutions at room temperature for 30 min in the absence of light. Finally, the images were captured using a Leica upright fluorescence microscope (DM6B).
2.9
HUVEC proliferation, migration, and tube formation assays
To evaluate proliferation, HUVECs (4 × 10
4
) were introduced to the lower chamber, while the upper chamber received 200 mg of ECM, 20 μg of ADSC-Exos, or a combination of both. Ki67 immunofluorescent staining was employed to assess HUVEC proliferation. Specifically, cells were washed thrice with PBS for 5 min each time, fixed with 4 % Paraformaldehyde for 15 min, and then washed thrice with PBS for 5 min each time. To enhance the permeability of the membrane, a 0.5 % (v/v) Triton X-100 in PBS solution was used to permeabilize the cells for a duration of 20 min. Subsequently, the cells were blocked with 1 % (v/v) goat serum for 60 min at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation at 4 °C with an antibody targeting Ki67. The following day, the cells were subjected to a 2-h incubation with phalloidin staining solution and secondary antibody. Finally, the cells were washed and stained with DAPI for 5 min, and the samples were visualized using fluorescence microscopy.
For the migration assays, 4 × 10
4
HUVECs were introduced to the upper chamber of a Transwell assay filter. The lower chamber was supplemented with 200 mg of ECM, 20 μg of ADSC-Exos, or a combination of both. The cells were cultured for 18 h at 37 °C, followed by fixation and staining of the cells on the upper chamber membrane using 0.5 % crystal violet for subsequent microscopic quantification.
To assess the impact of ADSC-Exos on HUVEC tube formation, HUVECs were cultured in DMEM extraction solutions of varying compositions for a duration of 6 h. Subsequently, the morphological alterations of HUVECs were examined under a microscope. Matrigel (50 μL) was placed in a 96-well plate and allowed to solidify at 37 °C for 30 min. HUVECs (0.8 × 10
4
cells/100 μL) were suspended in serum-free medium and added to the Matrigel-coated wells. The cell suspensions were then incubated at 37 °C and 5 % CO
2
for 24 h. The specimen was subjected to observation and photographic documentation under an optical microscope at hourly intervals until the conclusion of the experiment. The quantification and measurement of tube lengths were conducted using ImageJ software and subjected to statistical analysis via the ANOVA-test.
The Transwell assay filters were utilized in a co-culture system to evaluate the proliferation, migration, and tube formation capacity of HUVECs.
2.10
Animal model
The Experimental Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine granted approval for the animal experiments, with license number (2020) No. (139). A total of 30 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (SD rats; average weight 250 g), procured from the Experimental Animal Institute of Medical College of Zhejiang University, were randomly assigned to five groups: Blank (n = 6), Control (n = 6), ADSC-Exos (n = 6), ECM (n = 6), and ECM@ ADSC-Exos (n = 6). A model of rodent thin endometrium was established by means of injecting anhydrous ethanol into the uterus, as previously described. In brief, all rats were subjected to anesthesia via intraperitoneal injection of 2 % sodium pentobarbital (0.3 mL/100 g), and the uterine horns were exposed through an abdominal incision. The proximal and distal portions of the uterus were subsequently clamped with two vascular clamps, following which 95 % ethanol was injected into the uterine cavity for a duration of 60 s. Blank group animals were injected with 100 μL PBS in the uterine horn. The vascular clamps were subsequently released and delicately compressed to eliminate any residual ethanol, and the affected areas were rinsed with PBS thrice to further eliminate any remaining ethanol. The experimental group of animals underwent reoperation after model development, wherein one end of the uterus was clipped, and the experimental group materials were injected into the uterine cavity via syringe from the other end. ADSC-Exos group was injected with 100 μL PBS containing 10 μg of ADSC-Exos; ECM group injection 100 μL PBS containing 100 mg of ECM; ECM@ ADSC-Exos group injection 100 μL PBS containing 100 mg of ECM@ADSC-Exos. Following the injection of materials, the rats underwent three estrus cycles before being euthanized, and their uterine tissues were excised and sectioned or frozen as appropriate for downstream analyses.
2.11
Histological evaluation
The assessment of endometrial fibrosis involved initial fixation of excised tissue sections in 4 % paraformaldehyde for an overnight period, followed by demineralization utilizing 16 % ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, and subsequent embedding in OCT. The sections were then subjected to routine H&E and Masson's trichrome staining.
2.12
Immunohistochemical staining
The present study utilized immunohistochemical staining to evaluate the levels of endometrial fibrosis and angiogenesis. Specifically, 20 μm-thick sections were initially blocked with 5 % BSA, and subsequently incubated overnight with rabbit anti-CD31 (1:100; ab28364, Abcam) and rabbit anti-α-SMA (1:100; ab108531, Abcam) at 4 °C. Following three washes with PBS, the sections were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with secondary goat anti-rabbit IgG, and finally observed under an optical microscope.
2.13
Fertility testing
The evaluation of endometrial receptivity was predicated on the capacity of the endometrium to facilitate the implantation of a fertilized embryo and to provide adequate nourishment for fetal development. The rat estrus cycle status was determined through a vaginal smear method. Twenty female rats were selected from each of the five treatment groups outlined above and were subjected to mating with sexually mature male rats at a 1:1 ratio on the day of estrus. The presence or absence of a vaginal plug was subsequently evaluated the following morning. At 18 days post vaginal plug appearance, fetal numbers, size, and weight were assessed in each group, as were embryo locations.
2.14
Statistical analysis
Data in the present study were expressed as mean ± S.D. (standard deviation), and
p
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical evaluation was performed by one-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey test for multiple comparisons.

3.1
Preparation and characterizations of decellularized ECM
Porcine dermis tissue was processed to remove the cellular components accordingly to previous studies in order to obtained porcine dermis derived ECM[
21
]. FE-SEM observation showed that ECM exhibited a filamentous and porous microstructure, and the filaments were arranged in a bundled pattern, which was similar to native ECM arrangement in the normal tissue (
Fig. 2
A). HE staining results demonstrated that after decellularization, nucleated cells were eliminated while the structural organization of dermis ECM was successfully preserved (
Fig. 2
B). The decellularization efficiency was also verified by DNA quantification. Only a trace amount of DNA content was detected in the decellularized ECM compared with non-decellularized tissue (
Fig. 2
C). Besides, fat content was also reduced by decellularization process (
Fig. 2
D). As shown in
Fig. 2
E, the collagen content in the ECM was around 80 %, confirming that active components of ECM were preserved after decellularization. Since abundant binding domains were found on collagen to orchestrate growth factor binding, distribution, and signal transduction, high collagen content in the ECM may play important roles during tissue regeneration. The data presented in
Fig. 2
F demonstrates that the decellularization process effectively retains a significant quantity of active growth factors within the tissue, thereby validating its safety. The presence of these active factors within the ECM highlighted its potential to facilitate tissue regeneration by releasing active factors during the degradation process. The biodegradation of intrauterine biomaterials is a crucial attribute, prompting us to assess the in vitro biodegradation of extracellular matrix (ECM). Our observations in SBF revealed that approximately 40 % of the ECM underwent degradation within 40 days (
Fig. 2
G), reaching a plateau thereafter. The remaining scaffold was inferred to be a more stable collagen component. Upon treatment with type I Collagenase, complete degradation of the scaffold was achieved (
Fig. 2
H), thereby confirming our inference and demonstrating the exceptional
in vivo
degradation performance of ECM. The proteomic analysis revealed that ECM contained mainly extracellular matrix structural proteins, extracellular matrix proteoglycan, extracellular fluid proteins and a small proportion of intracellular proteins, and these proteins had interrelated actions with each other, indicating the complexity and integrity of ECM was preserved during processing (
Fig. 2
I and J).

Angiogenetic effects of ADSC-Exos, ECM and ECM@ADSC-Exos
Angiogenesis is one of the crucial steps of tissue repair after acute injury. Integral vascularization guarantees sufficiency blood supply to the wounded area and facilitated tissue repair
[25]
. It has been reported that MSC-derived exosomes could promote tissue angiogenesis when delivered to injured tissue regions. Besides, considerable amount of VEGF was also detected in ECM, suggesting ECM might also be capable of promoting angiogenesis. Therefore, we conducted a series of assays including Ki67, migration assay and tube formation to evaluate the angiogenetic effect of ADSC-Exos, ECM and ECM@ADSC-Exos. Ki67 immunofluorescence staining results showed that ADSC-Exos, ECM and ECM@ADSC-Exo all promoted HUVEC proliferation compared to control; moreover, ki67+ HUVECs of ECM@ADSC-Exos group were more abundant than those of ADSC-Exos group or ECM group (

Fig. 5
C and D. Angiogenesis is an important step of the early tissue repair. Therefore, we performed immunohistochemistry staining of CD31, an indicator of angiogenesis, to evaluate angiogenesis in different groups.

4
Discussion
In this study, we successfully constructed an ADSC-derived exosome-coupled ECM delivery system to achieve sustained release of functional exosomes while providing scaffolding layer on the surface of inured uterine, leading to regeneration of functional endometrium. Both in vitro and
in vivo
experiments proved the regenerative effects of ECM@ADSC-Exos by showing sustained release of functional exosomes, more active endothelial cell migration and proliferation, fully regeneration of injured endometrium, and successful implantation of healthy embryos.
ECM has been regarded as an ideal biomaterial for tissue regeneration due to its natural origin, high similarity to native tissue, and bioactive component preservation. However, immune rejection against xenogeneic components remains to be a major problem needed to overcome. In our research, a systematic decellularization process was introduced to remove the cellular components while exquisitely preserving the main bioactive components of ECM. HE staining before and after decellularization proved that we successfully removed cells from the tissue, and DNA remnant measurement further confirmed cell depletion. VEGF determination indicated that VEGF was relatively enriched in decellularized ECM. Proteomic analysis showed that our decellularized ECM mainly contains ECM structure protein and ECM proteoglycans (
Fig. 2
). ADSC-exos were also isolated and characterized by SEM, flow cytometry and western blotting (
Fig. 3
).
Cytocompatibility is one major concern of implanted biomaterials. Our results indicated that ECM@ADSC-exos did not have cytotoxicity, but could promoted HUVEC proliferation in vitro. Besides, when suspended in saline, ECM exhibited good injectability, making it convenient and less invasive to be delivered into uterine cavity. Moreover, in vitro degradation observation showed that ECM showed good biodegradation (
Fig. 2
) in SBF; when implanted in the uterine cavity, it could not be observed after 3 estrus cycles, leaving the uterine cavity unobstructed (
Fig. 6
).
Delivery of exogenous stem cells or stem cell derived exosomes has been shown effective in promoting endometrium regeneration. However, effective retention at target sites of these biologics is very challenging because such fluidic formulation could be easily discharged due to the uterine spontaneous contraction. ECM proteins such as collagen, fibronectin and elastin possess natural motifs for biomacromolecule immobilization. Decellularized ECM retained most of the structure of the natural ECM components, therefore, it could easily adhere to the injured surface of the endometrium. When ADSC-Exos were loaded into ECM, these exosomes were successfully loaded on its surface. When decellularized ECM was injected and attached to the uterine surface, these exosomes could achieve local release and affect their surrounding cells. ECM was rich in positively charged groups while exosomes were negatively charged, thus exosomes could be effectively coupled onto the ECM by electrostatic interactions, thereby efficiently delivered into and sustainably released in the uterine cavity.
Angiogenesis is one of the prerequisites for tissue regeneration as tissues can only survive within a small range of vasculature. The endometrium regeneration outcomes positively correlated with the angiogenesis extent in each group (
Fig. 5
). In vitro results showed that ECM and ADSC-exos promoted HUVEC growth, migration and enhanced HUVEC tube formation, indicating these components of our system played a significant role in term of angiogenesis (
Fig. 5
). Studies have also revealed that miRNAs contained in MSC-derived exosomes activated angiogenesis and enhanced tissue repair[
26
]. Our results demonstrated that VEGF was relatively enriched in the obtained ECM(
Fig. 2
) and our previous study even demonstrated that the processed ECM possessed abundant motifs for various growth factor binding and storage[
22
]. The angiogenic components of both ADSC-exos and ECM when coupled together leveraging their affinity with each other brought the better angiogenesis and endometrium regeneration in this research.
Myometrium, the smooth muscle layer beneath endometrium, serves as important foundation for uterine function. It provides most of the mechanical strength to support embryo growth during pregnancy and the contraction force to deliver the fetus during parturition. Besides, myometrial cells facilitate in maintaining endometrium MSCs hemostasis [
27
]. Weakness or defect of the myometrium is also associated with high spontaneous abortion rate during pregnancy and might cause uterine rupture [
23
]. Therefore, myometrium regeneration is also crucial for in female fertility restoration. HE staining of the injured uterus showed that ethanol injury caused focal necrosis in rat myometrium (
Fig. 6
) as indicated by decreased αSMA expression in the control group. In the treated groups, the αSMA expression levels were significantly higher than the control group. These results indicated that ADSC-exos when coupled with ECM also restored myometrium morphology and function, which might be another important aspect of endometrium healing.
The ultimate goal of the endometrium regeneration is fertility restoration, which was demonstrated by successful embryo implantation in the treated groups in our research (
Fig. 7
). Another thing that deserves specifical attention is whether the treatments will bring side effects to the offspring. Since the injected ECM@ADSC-exos was totally degraded before embryo implantation, we could reasonably conclude that the implanted material has only little or no direct effects on embryo development. By our crude observation, no morphological developmental defects were observed in the fetuses in the ECM@ADSC-exos group, which consisted with previous researches[
[14]
,
[24]
].
5
Conclusion
In this study, we prepared a decellularized ECM scaffold. Characterization results proved good efficacy of decellularization and excellent cytocompatibility. To prepare ECM@ADSC-exos, we isolated, characterized and load ADSC-exos on the decellularized ECM. Animal experiment results showed that ECM@ADSC-exos intrauterine implantation could significantly improve endometrium thickness, angiogenesis, myometrium regeneration and finally restored fertility. Overall, this study indicated that ECM@ADSC-exos could be a novel option for endometrium repair in the future.
